parakeet: The tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised. And coming out of the tombs after his resurrection, they entered the holy city and appeared to many. Now, Matthew reports that at the moment of Jesus' death and in connection with his resurrection, a cascade of extraordinary events occurred simultaneously. The temple veil was torn in two, an earthquake split rocks, tombs were opened, and many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep were raised. These resurrected individuals are said to have entered Jerusalem and appeared to many people. This is not described as a private vision, symbolic experience, or isolated miracle. It's presented as a public, physical, multiperson resurrection event occurring in Jerusalem during Roman occupation at one of the most politically volatile moments of the year. If this happened as described, the scene would have been unmistakable and profoundly destabilizing. Recently deceased individuals known to families, neighbors, and communities would be walking openly through the city. These would not be anonymous figures, they would be identifiable people with burial histories, funerals, and social memory. Jerusalem, already tense during Passover and under heavy Roman surveillance, would erupt into chaos. Roman authorities would intervene immediately, temple leadership would be forced to respond publicly, and the event would eclipse the crucifixion itself in significance. This would not be a marginal detail or a symbolic flourish. It would be the most disruptive public event in first century Judea. If Matthew's account were literal history, several consequences would follow almost immediately.
